title: The Marcos family has a knack for banning video games

blocks.text: CEBU, Philippines — Does the Marcos family have something against video games? I ask simply because the father and the son seem to have a knack for banning them during their respective presidential terms.

The Philippine government has been mulling over banning certain video games and related platforms. Why? That’s because they have been cited as a factor in recent school shooting incidents. Basically, they say video games equal violence.

But this is not the first time video games have been banned in the Philippines. In fact, if you ask your lolos and lolas — or maybe one of your older uncles — they may recall the time when former President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., father of Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., banned video games back in the 1980s.
When Marcos Sr. banned video games during Martial Law
Two years after Martial Law was declared in 1972, Marcos Sr., through Presidential Decree No. 519, banned pinball, slot machines, and similar devices on July 23, 1974.

Several years later, Marcos Sr. then reinforced the ban through the Letter of Instruction No. 1176, s. 1981. The Letter of Instruction, at the height of Martial Law, was addressed to the Minister of Finance, Cesar Virata, and the Minister of National Defense, Juan Ponce Enrile.

Originally, the 1974 ban specifically targeted pinball and slot machines. Video games were later added to the ban via the Letter of Instruction, as they fell under the category of “similar contrivances.”
People who owned or operated these machines were only given 15 days to destroy or dismantle them or turn them over to the police. At the time, the police were called the Philippine Constabulary.
Video games were called ‘video machines’ at the time, and are most likely referring to the coin-operated arcade versions.
Furthermore, during the 80s, home consoles were slowly becoming popular, with Nintendo Game & Watch units being a massive cultural hit that spawned a street-rental culture.

Marcos Sr. said that video games, or video machines “tends to corrupt the children and other youth of school age and encourages juvenile delinquency, drug addiction, petty thievery, lying and the gambling instinct which may lead to idleness, economic waste and dislike for work.”
The Letter of Instruction revealed that this sentiment was echoed by multiple civic groups, concerned parents, teachers, and citizens through numerous petitions sent to the Office of the President.
The blanket ban on video games was effectively lifted when the EDSA People Power Revolution in 1986 ended Marcos Sr.’s tenure as president.
The Philippines was not the only Southeast Asian state to have banned video games in their country in the 80s.
Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia had some sort of arcade crackdowns in their respective countries during the decade.

Another Marcos banning video games

Fast forward more than four decades, and video games are once again part of a national conversation about youth, violence, and public safety. Now, the possibility of banning them falls under Marcos Jr.’s presidency.
The clamor to ban video games again resurfaced following the June 2026 school shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, where three students were killed and others were injured.
This time, a specific game, GoreBox, was at the center of the controversy.
On June 23, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) announced a temporary ban on GoreBox while authorities investigated whether the game played any role in the incident.

The temporary ban on GoreBox was described as a precaution while the investigation into the case itself continued. Authorities did not establish a direct causal link between the game and the shooting at the time.

Nevertheless, GoreBox was eventually removed from Google Play and Steam in the Philippines. However, with Android Package Kits (APKs) and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), people can circumvent this and still download GoreBox.
Philippines banning video games
Besides GoreBox, other gaming-related platforms, as well as video games in general, have gotten targets on their backs too.

In July, Marcos Jr., said he was open to banning violent online games if evidence showed that they contributed to the desensitization of children to violence. He said violent video games desensitize minors to commit killing and violence.
He added that the government should first conduct a thorough assessment before deciding what policy response was appropriate.

“So, we’ll just continue what we’re doing. But of course, when it is clear that a certain game, or a class of games, is responsible for the desensitization of our children to violence, then yes, I think we should ban them. And we will ban them,” Marcos Jr. expressed.
Although the President said that earlier this year, the government’s scrutiny of video games and related platforms did not stop there.
On September 23, the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), through the CICC, temporarily blocked Discord in the Philippines.
Discord is a communication platform widely used by gaming communities for voice chats, text conversations, and organizing online community events.

After a day, the Discord ban was lifted after the platform’s representatives met with Philippine authorities and committed to strengthening the platform’s child-safety measures and cooperating with the government.
Same family, different eras

More than 40 years after Marcos Sr. argued that video machines could encourage juvenile delinquency and other social problems, his son is once again presiding over discussions about restricting violent video games and online platforms.
But the similarities end there.

One key difference between the two is that Marcos Sr. personally ordered the ban on video games, while Marcos Jr. has not directly imposed such bans. Instead, recent restrictions and proposals have come from government agencies under Marcos Jr.’s administration, like the DICT and the CICC.
And with the short-lived Discord ban, the conversation has now moved beyond games themselves and toward the wider online communities and platforms that the youth use.
So, do the Marcoses have something against video games?
That might make for a catchy headline.

But the bigger story is how the Philippine government continues to grapple with an increasingly complicated question: Where should it draw the line between protecting young people from harmful online content and restricting access to the digital spaces where an entire generation now plays, communicates, and socializes?
For Filipino gamers, that is a question worth asking, as this time the debate is no longer happening inside the arcade.
